procedural_history.originating_court: Court of 3rd Additional District Judge at 24-Parganas
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Decree dated the 5th day of March, 1951 of the High Court of Judicature at Calcutta in Appeal from Original Decree No. 87 of 1949 arising out of the decree dated the 20th day of January, 1949 in Suit No. 94 of 1946
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court heard an appeal (No. 87 of 1949) from the original decree of the District Judge. The High Court directed the cases to be tried by a competent court, because they believed they had lost jurisdiction after January 26, 1950.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court held that the special court under Act XII of 1952 had jurisdiction and that the proceedings before it should not be quashed. The Supreme Court also rejected the appellant's contention regarding the attestation of the will, finding that the High Court's conclusion was based on a consideration of all the materials and should be accepted.

issue.issue_text: Whether the proceedings before the special court under Act XII of 1952 should be quashed for lack of jurisdiction.

facts: The High Court lost its own jurisdiction to try the cases after January 26, 1950.
The High Court then directed that the cases be tried by a 'competent court'.
The original Special Tribunal, constituted under Ordinance XXIX of 1943, was no longer a competent court to which the cases could be sent back.
law: The court considered whether the jurisdiction of the special court, established under Act XII of 1952, was ousted by Section 12 of that Act or by the High Court's order.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that since the High Court could no longer try the cases and the old Special Tribunal was defunct, the only competent court available to try the cases was the special court created under Act XII of 1952.
The High Court's order, which required a trial by a competent court, was interpreted as supporting the jurisdiction of this new special court, as it was the only viable option.
The Court found that neither Section 12 of the Act nor the High Court's order removed (ousted) the jurisdiction of the special court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the special court under Act XII of 1952 had proper jurisdiction to hear the cases, and therefore, the proceedings before it should not be quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a will can be considered not duly attested as a matter of law, as required by s. 63 of the Indian Succession Act, simply because the attesting witnesses did not explicitly state in their examination-in-chief that they signed the will in the presence of the testator.

facts: The two attesting witnesses testified in their examination-in-chief that the testator signed the will in their presence and that they attested his signature.
However, the witnesses did not explicitly state that they signed the will in the presence of the testator.
The appellant argued that this omission meant the will was not duly attested as a matter of law, as required by s. 63 of the Indian Succession Act.
The execution and attestation of the will took place during a single sitting at the residence of one of the witnesses, where all parties had gathered by appointment.
The witnesses were not cross-examined on the specific question of whether they signed in the testator's presence.
law: The Supreme Court held that it cannot be laid down as a matter of law that a will is not duly attested simply because the attesting witnesses did not explicitly state in their examination-in-chief that they signed in the presence of the testator.
Whether the attesting witnesses signed in the presence of the testator is a pure question of fact that depends on the appreciation of the evidence and the specific circumstances of each case.
application: The Court rejected the appellant's argument for a rigid legal rule, instead treating the issue as a question of fact to be inferred from the circumstances.

The High Court, whose reasoning was accepted, inferred that due attestation occurred because the entire process of execution and attestation took place at one pre-arranged meeting. It was logical to conclude that everyone remained present until the matter was finished.
The Supreme Court also noted that the witnesses were not cross-examined on this point, which weakened the appellant's challenge.
The Court accepted the lower courts' finding of fact that the will was duly attested, as this finding was based on a consideration of all the materials and circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention and held that the will was duly attested. The Court decided that the failure of attesting witnesses to explicitly state in their examination-in-chief that they signed in the testator's presence does not automatically invalidate the will as a matter of law; rather, due attestation can be inferred as a matter of fact from the overall evidence and circumstances of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the will in question was executed under undue influence and pressure.

facts: The testator was in full possession of his mental faculties and had the required testamentary capacity.
The will was a holograph will, meaning it was written entirely by the testator himself.
The testator personally made all arrangements for the will's execution and registration.
The first respondent, who was the main beneficiary, had no role in the preparation, execution, or registration of the will.
After execution, the testator kept the will in his personal cash box.
The testator lived for nearly a year after executing the will, and despite discussing it, he affirmed that it should stand.
The only evidence of influence was testimony that the first respondent told the testator he could not live under the same roof as the appellant (his brother).
The appellant, who alleged undue influence, accepted payments of a legacy under the will for 15 months after the testator's death.
law: Once it is proven that a will was executed with proper formalities by a person of competent understanding, the burden of proving undue influence falls on the person who alleges it.
Not all influence is 'undue'. Persuasion, appeals to affection, or a person pleading their case to the testator are legitimate and do not invalidate a will.
Undue influence requires pressure, fraud, or coercion that is so significant it overpowers the testator's volition and takes away their free agency.
If the testator retains their mental capacity and there is no fraud or coercion, a will cannot be successfully challenged on the grounds of undue influence.
application: The Court determined that the burden of proof was on the appellant, as the testator's mental competence was not in dispute.
The Court found no evidence that the first respondent did anything to affect the testator's free will. In fact, the evidence showed the first respondent was not involved in the will's creation.

The Court considered the testimony about the first respondent's statements as a legitimate expression of his views, which the testator was free to accept or reject. This did not amount to coercion that overpowered the testator's judgment.

The cumulative effect of the evidence—the will being a holograph, the testator arranging everything himself, his reaffirmation of the will, and keeping it in his possession—strongly indicated that the will was an expression of his own free volition.
The Court also noted that the appellant's own actions in accepting benefits under the will weakened his claim that it was invalid.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the will was not the result of undue influence. The evidence clearly established that the will represented the free volition of the testator, and therefore, the Court rejected the challenge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a will can be considered not duly attested as a matter of law, as required by s. 63 of the Indian Succession Act, simply because the attesting witnesses did not explicitly state in their examination-in-chief that they signed the will in the presence of the testator.
appellant_arguments: The will should be held void because there was no proof of due attestation as required by section 63 of the Indian Succession Act.

The attesting witnesses, in their examination-in-chief, stated that the testator signed in their presence and that they attested his signature, but they did not explicitly state that they signed the will in the presence of the testator.
In the absence of such explicit evidence, it must be held as a matter of law that there was no due attestation.
respondent_arguments: Due attestation can be properly inferred from the circumstances, such as the execution and attestation taking place at one sitting where the testator and witnesses had assembled by appointment.
The fact of due execution and attestation was not challenged on behalf of the caveator (appellant) during the hearing of the suit in the lower court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the will in question was executed under undue influence and pressure.
appellant_arguments: Although the recitals in the will disinheriting the son (appellant) might have reflected the testator's feelings years ago, by the time the will was executed, the testator's natural affection for his son had re-asserted itself.
The testator had forgiven and forgotten the past, and the will did not correctly reflect his state of mind at the time of execution.
Correspondence between the testator and the appellant's family shows the testator was solicitous about the appellant's welfare, indicating a change of heart.
respondent_arguments: Not every influence on a testator is 'undue'; it is permissible to persuade a testator to make a disposition in one's favour.
The testator was in full possession of his mental faculties and there was no element of fraud or coercion.
The respondent had no role in the preparation, execution, or registration of the will.
The will was a holograph will, the testator made all arrangements himself, registered it, and kept it in his possession.
The testator lived for nearly a year after executing the will and, despite discussing it, affirmed that it should stand.
The appellant himself accepted a legacy under the will for 15 months, which is inconsistent with the claim of undue influence.

cases.principle: For the legal principle defining undue influence, stating that a testator may be led, but not driven, and the will must be the product of the testator's own volition, not someone else's.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is not every influence brought to bear on a testator that can be characterized as 'undue'; a person may plead their cause and persuade a testator to make a disposition in their favor. Furthermore, it cannot be laid down as a matter of law that there was no due attestation simply because the attesting witnesses did not explicitly state in their examination-in-chief that they signed the will in the presence of the testator. Whether the attesting witnesses signed in the presence of the testator is a pure question of fact to be determined by an appreciation of the evidence and circumstances of the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that the due attestation of a will is a pure question of fact that can be inferred from the circumstances of its execution, and it cannot be invalidated as a matter of law simply because the attesting witnesses did not explicitly state in their examination-in-chief that they signed in the testator's presence. The court also found that the special court had proper jurisdiction to hear the case, as it was the only competent court available after a High Court order determined that the original tribunal could not proceed.
legal_tests_applied: Whether attesting witnesses signed in the presence of the testator is not a matter of law requiring a specific statement, but is a 'pure question of fact depending on appreciation of evidence' and the circumstances of the case.

For a will to be invalid due to undue influence, there must be 'pressure of whatever character, whether acting on the fears or the hopes, if so exerted as to overpower the volition without convincing the judgment.' Legitimate influences such as persuasion or appeals to affection are permissible.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the proceedings should be quashed for lack of jurisdiction, finding that the special court was the only competent court that could try the cases after the High Court's order, and its jurisdiction was not otherwise ousted.

The court rejected the argument that the will was not duly attested as a matter of law, stating that the absence of a specific statement from witnesses that they signed in the testator's presence is not fatal. The court deferred to the lower courts' factual finding that due attestation could be inferred from the circumstances, especially since the issue was not cross-examined or challenged during the original hearing.
why_respondent_won: The jurisdiction of the special court was upheld because it was the only competent court to try the cases, and its jurisdiction was not ousted by section 12 of the Act or by the order of the High Court.

The finding that the will was duly attested was upheld because it is a question of fact, and the lower courts properly inferred due attestation from the circumstances that the execution and attestation took place at one sitting where all parties were assembled. The failure of the appellant to challenge this fact at trial further weakened their position.
